messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

At seventy-four, Mai still moves with the precision of the software engineer she has been for five decades, her mind a place of logic and order. It is a structure she has clung to, a fortress against a chaos that first broke in forty years ago and has never truly left. The trauma was not a single moment but a series of escalating terrors revolving around her son, then six years old, and a sudden, catastrophic asthma attack that silenced his breathing. That silence is what she remembers most. The frantic, high-pitched whine of their car engine as her husband sped to the hospital, the acrid, sterile smell of the emergency room that clung to her clothes for days, and then, in the pediatric ICU, the sudden, terrible quiet when the rhythmic beep of his heart monitor flatlined.

The triggers from that time remain potent and unpredictable. Mai works from home, and the sudden lulls in her quiet suburban street can be unbearable. A moment of complete silence will descend, and she is instantly back in that hospital room, the same cold terror seizing her chest as she watches the straight green line on the monitor. The memory arrives not as a clear image, but as a full-body sensation of dread and a crushing wave of shame. She is convinced the event happened because of how she acted; she missed the signs, she didn't get him to the doctor sooner, her failure is etched into the memory of that silence. The sound of a car accelerating quickly down her street can have the same effect, plunging her back into the desperate race to the hospital and reinforcing her belief that she is fundamentally helpless to stop bad things from happening.

These deeply held convictions—that the world is a dangerous place and she is powerless within it—have become the lens through which she views her life. This internal narrative of helplessness and self-blame fuels a constant, exhausting state of threat. Mai finds it nearly impossible to fall asleep, certain that she must remain alert for any sign of danger to her husband, her now-grown son, or her grandchildren. She lies awake for hours, cataloging every creak of the house, every distant siren, her body rigid with a hypervigilance that offers no rest. She feels as though her watchfulness is the only thing standing between her family and another disaster, a penance for her past perceived failures.

This state of perpetual high alert makes her exquisitely sensitive to the very cues that torment her, creating a vicious, self-sustaining cycle. Because she is always on guard, her mind scans her environment for confirmation of danger, inevitably finding it in the triggers she most fears. The ordinary quiet of her home is no longer peaceful but a portent of doom, an auditory vacuum waiting to be filled by tragedy. This heightened threat-state primes her mind to access the traumatic memories, so that being watchful leads directly back to the terror and shame of the past. Her memories, in turn, reinforce her negative appraisals; each time she is ambushed by the feeling of that hospital room, it serves as fresh evidence of her own culpability and the world’s inherent danger, tightening the loop of fear.

Over the years, Mai’s world has shrunk. She avoids hospitals, even for her own check-ups, and makes excuses to not visit friends or family if it requires a long drive on the freeway. Her husband worries about her profound exhaustion, and her son feels the persistent hum of her anxiety whenever they are together. The breaking point came last month during a family dinner. In a moment of easy, comfortable silence around the table, Mai was suddenly overwhelmed by a wave of pure, imageless terror so profound she gasped for air, frightening her grandchildren. There was no picture in her mind, only the raw feeling of absolute dread and shame, disconnected from any context. It was this experience—the fear that she was losing control, that the trauma could consume her without warning—that finally propelled her to seek help. She wants to believe peace is possible, but is terrified that if she ever truly lets her guard down, the silence will finally claim something she cannot bear to lose.
